s: Bihanic, youngest of three brothers, is sent by a king to rob a giant’s treasures. Disguised as a sheep, he enters the castle, kills the giantess cook, takes the oracular parrot, and flees.

consist_of oracular parrot [among other treasures] The giant’s treasures consist of an oracular parrot, a swift dromedary, and a carbuncle whose light illuminates the night for seven leagues. Bihanic obtains the dromedary and carbuncle relatively easily and later steals the parrot.

has gift of second sight [wonderful] The oracular parrot possesses the gift of second sight and is consulted by the giant morning and evening. It identifies Bihanic as the giant’s enemy and reveals that he is hiding in the sheepfold, but Bihanic ultimately captures it.
A poor widow lives in a cottage with her son and daughter, warns her son of Ogres' land, then consents to their journey and gives her daughter a little silver cross.

is_a Christian The boy decides to seek his fortune by gathering golden horns in the land of the Ogres. After an Ogre captures him and his sister, he talks to delay his fate, blinds the Ogre with a glowing brand, disguises himself in a sheep's skin and golden horns, and escapes the cave.
A Christian girl guards her brother with a silver cross, is roasted and swallowed by an ogre, emerges alive when vomited up, and returns with him to their mother.

Giants are seven fathoms tall one-eyed Ogres living in the land of the Ogres, with Ogre brothers. They tend golden-horned oxen and sheep, capture and roast Christians alive, then swallow them in one bite in caves of a wild black country.
The Ogres capture and eat Christians. The boy and girl are called little Christians by the Ogre, and the boy says that Christians do not eat one another.

l: land of the Ogres, The Library
s: Far from the children's home toward the setting sun, the land of the Ogres contains wild black country, mountains, waterfalls, golden-horned oxen and sheep, and no priests.
A mountainous region with streams falling from heights of three thousand feet, inhabited by Ogres and lacking priests, churches, and churchyards.

is_a cave [home of an Ogre] The Ogre's cave is closed by a massive stone and contains the Ogre, the children, and cattle with golden horns. The boy hides there, blinds the Ogre, waits three days and nights, and escapes when the entrance is opened for the hungry cattle.

is_a group of priests [seven in number] They form by joining one another during their journey. A Cyclops captures them, eats one, and is then blinded by the other six, who escape disguised in sheep skins.
A small silver cross, given by a poor widow to a girl who carries it, is held as the girl prays while being roasted alive.
Golden horns from Ogres’ oxen and sheep are discarded after cattle are killed; children collect a hundred, gain riches, and the boy uses sheep’s horns in disguise.
The Ogres use a gridiron to roast captured Christians. The girl is laid on one and roasted alive over a slow fire.

l: flat stone (the cave entrance stone), The Library
s: weighs a hundred hundredweights [shuts the cave entrance] The cave entrance is blocked by a flat stone weighing a hundred hundredweights. The Ogre moves it with his shoulder, and later the boy cannot move it; the stone finally falls when the Ogre opens the cave for the cattle.

l: journey to the land of the Ogres, The Library
s: A boy and girl’s seven-month journey toward the setting sun, sustained by alms and stable lodgings, ends in the land of the Ogres.

l: search for golden horns, The Library
s: A boy and girl spend seven days searching mountains for golden horns, hiding among bushes and rocks, fill wallets with a hundred horns, then return home.

l: capture of the children, The Library
s: is_performed_by Ogre [the children are put in a big bag] An Ogre sees the children while driving his oxen and sheep and throws them into a big bag. He carries them to his cave and orders them to turn the spit while he prepares a meal.

l: roasting of the girl, The Library
s: Ogre, enraged by a girl's prayer to God, strips her, roasts her alive on a gridiron over a slow fire, then swallows her whole.

l: blinding of the Ogre, The Library
s: is_performed_by boy [with a glowing brand thrust into the Ogre's eye] After the Ogre falls asleep, the boy takes a glowing brand from the hearth and thrusts it into the Ogre's eye. The Ogre becomes blind and cries out that he is blind.

l: escape from the cave, The Library
s: is_performed_by boy [disguised with a sheep's skin and golden horns] The boy hides among the cattle and later disguises himself with a sheep's skin and golden horns. He passes among the sheep as the blind Ogre counts them, then runs away when the Ogre suspects him.

l: vomiting up the girl, The Library
s: is_performed_by Ogre [the girl is vomited up alive] The Ogre becomes sick and vomits up the girl alive after swallowing her. This allows the girl to leave with her brother.
A tale in which a boy and girl escape the land of the Ogres and return to their mother with riches from golden horns.
It is presented as a possible means by which the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus has survived, particularly in Sicily.
Two monks, beggars travelling for the church, include a large and small monk; lost in a monster’s cave, the large is killed, while the small escapes to Trapani.

escapes_from monster (Sicilian cave) [by hiding in a sheep's skin] He survives after the monster kills the larger monk. He pretends to eat the roasted flesh, blinds the monster with a heated iron, escapes in a sheep’s skin, and tells fishermen at Trapani what happened.
A monster inhabiting a cave traps two monks, kills and roasts the larger, tries to force the small monk to eat him, is blinded, releases sheep, fishes, and dies by breaking his head on a rock.

has_entrance_blocked_by monster (Sicilian cave) [with a great stone] It is the place where the two monks find the monster, are trapped by a great stone, and where the small monk blinds the monster and escapes.
is_in Cappadocia It is the place in Cappadocia where a Greek version of the story was recorded.
It is the region associated with the Greek story recorded at Pharasa.

l: Greek story of the seven priests, The Library
s: is_a Greek story [recorded at Pharasa] It tells of seven priests captured by a Cyclops. Six priests blind him with a heated spit, escape in sheep skins, take his sheep, and distribute them among themselves and the wife of the priest who was eaten.
A one-eyed giant with seven hundred sheep seizes seven priests, eats one, is blinded by six, and fails to detect their escape under sheep skins.
A prince enters an Ogre’s cave, eats milk and cake, blinds the sleeping Ogre with a heated stake, and escapes clinging to a ram’s belly.
A one-eyed giant inhabiting a cave returns with sheep, finds food missing and sleeps; a prince blinds him with a sharpened stake, and he releases sheep by touch while other Ogres leave him alone.
is_a island [off the west coast of Chios] It is the island off the west coast of Chios where a version told to Ludwig Ross was recorded.
He is one of three brothers who enter a magnificent palace. The blind Ogre seizes him and dashes him to pieces.
He is one of three brothers who enter the Ogre’s palace. The blind Ogre seizes him and dashes him to pieces.

escapes_from blind Ogre (Psara story) [hidden in a ram's skin] He escapes the blind Ogre by killing a ram, hiding in its skin, and passing through the gate among the sheep. The Ogre strokes his back but does not recognize him.
Three brothers land on an unknown coast; an Ogre kills Dimitri and Michael, while George escapes a palace in a ram’s skin.
is_a Ogre [huge, ugly, and blind] He appears at the palace, smells human flesh, and kills Dimitri and Michael. He lets George escape because he mistakes him for a ram.

l: Albanian version of the story, The Library
s: is_recorded_in Sicily It tells of two travellers captured by two Cyclopes with four eyes each. The travellers blind the Cyclopes with heated spits and escape in rams’ skins among the sheep.
They seek shelter in a cave during a storm and are held there for two days while the Cyclopes fatten them. They blind the Cyclopes and escape by disguising themselves in rams’ skins.

has four eyes [two eyes in front and two behind, each] They have two eyes in front and two behind and try to fatten and eat the two travellers. After being blinded, they guard the cave’s doors and fail to recognize the disguised men among the sheep.

is_used_by two travellers (Albanian story) [as disguises] They are used by the two travellers in the Albanian story as disguises during their escape from the Cyclopes. Similar sheep skins are used by the six priests in the Pharasa story.

l: Hungarian story of the giant, The Library
s: is_a story [Hungarian] It concerns three travelling craftsmen who find a one-eyed giant in a sheep stall. After the giant kills Balzer, Laurence and John blind him and escape by passing beneath sheep.
He is one of three travelling craftsmen in the Hungarian story. The giant identifies him as the fattest, cuts off his head, and gives him to the sheep.
He is one of the three travelling craftsmen. After the giant is blinded, he escapes by following John’s plan and using an awl while passing through the doorway beneath a sheep.
He is a shoemaker among the three travelling craftsmen. He blinds the giant with a firebrand and escapes with Laurence by using an awl and passing beneath sheep.
Three craftsmen sail seven days and nights; at a wood and sheep stall, giant kills Balzer; Laurence and John blind him and escape.

has one eye [in its forehead] He has one eye in his forehead and lives in a sheep stall sealed by a great stone. He kills Balzer, is blinded by John, and is later torn to pieces by twelve other giants.

is_a version of the old tale [Syrian] It tells of a youth who encounters a blind giant in a cave and escapes beneath a he-goat. Unlike the other versions, the youth later recovers and restores the giant’s eyes.

is_a prince [son of a prince's father] He enters a cave after hearing someone cry and pricks the sleeping giant with a needle. He escapes beneath the belly of a he-goat and later recovers the giant’s lost eyes from a she-bear.
is_a giant [blind and sleeping in a cave] He sleeps in a cave and searches unsuccessfully for the Syrian prince after being pricked. The prince later restores his lost sight.

includes Third Voyage of Sindibad the Sailor It contains versions of the story in the Third Voyage of Sindibad the Sailor and The Story of Seyf El-Mulook. These versions include giants who roast captives and are blinded with heated spits.

l: Third Voyage of Sindibad the Sailor, The Library
s: features Sindibad [as voyager] It tells of Sindibad and companions who encounter a giant that kills and eats several men. They blind him with red-hot spits and escape on rafts, though most are killed by rocks thrown by the giants.
He is among the travellers captured by the giant in the Third Voyage. He helps blind the giant with heated spits and escapes on a raft with two others.

is_a black monster [huge, with two eyes blazing like fire] He feels the travellers as a butcher feels sheep, kills and eats three of them over successive days, and sleeps afterward. Sindibad and the others blind him with red-hot spits before escaping.

l: The Story of Seyf El-Mulook, The Library
s: is_a story [included in The Arabian Nights] It contains a version in which Saed and memlooks encounter a giant who blinds captives with milk and eats roasted sheep. Saed avoids the milk, blinds the giant with heated spits, and kills him with a sword.

is_a brother of Seyf El-Mulook He is shipwrecked with memlooks and reaches a giant’s cave. He avoids being blinded by pretending to drink milk, blinds the giant with heated spits, and cuts him in half with a sword.

is_a giant [tall, with a long beard, long ears, and eyes like cressets] He keeps blinded men in his cave and blinds new captives by giving them milk. He roasts sheep, is blinded by Saed, and is cut in half with a sword.

l: blinding of the giant, The Library
s: A characteristic incident of the story type, the giant is blinded, commonly by a heated iron, stake, spit, firebrand, or coal. In one account, on the third evening a traveler thrusts a red-hot spit into his eye; the giant shrieks as the travelers run toward the sea. Some versions omit or reverse the blinding.

l: Story of the Eye in the Forehead, The Library
s: A widely current Armenian oral tale with several versions, it concerns a one-eyed giant who devours shipwrecked travelers until one traveler blinds him.
An oral popular tale current in Armenia, widely told in mountain towns and carried by emigrants, resembles the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus.

is_a wealthy man The rich man sees a porter carrying a sack of meal, has the sack sent to its destination, and invites the porter to dinner. He tells the porter and the other guests about his own difficult experience.
A porter carries a sack of meal and complains that his fate is horrible and unendurable while resting; a rich man invites him to dinner and asks him to judge whose lot is harder.
A merchant and handicraftsman sails on business with twenty companions, then alone survives a shipwreck, a giant's attack, and the destruction of a boat.
number twenty The merchant's twenty companions are shipwrecked with him and reach the shore. The one-eyed giant eats them one by one, and all are eventually drowned except the merchant.
A ship carrying a merchant and twenty companions is overtaken by a great storm, cast onto rocks, and broken apart.
is_a storm [destructive] The great storm overtakes the ship carrying the merchant and his companions. It casts the ship onto rocks and breaks it apart, while the wind carries the travelers ashore.

A one-eyed giant lives in a building in the wood, with an eye in the middle of his forehead. He kindles a fire with an oven, roasts victims on an iron spit, and eats one traveler each evening until the merchant's group blinds him.
is_blinded_by blinding of the giant [with a red-hot spit] The giant's eye is located in the middle of his forehead. It is pierced and blinded by a red-hot iron spit.
The iron spit is heated in the fire and thrust into the giant's eye on the merchant's advice. The attack blinds the giant and allows the travelers to flee.
are_eaten_by one-eyed giant [after being roasted] The giant's victims are the merchant's companions. He chooses the strongest and fattest among them, roasts them on a spit, and eats them.

is_a cannibal feast [involving the shipwrecked men] The giant's cannibal feast takes place each evening after he returns from walking about. He selects one traveler, roasts him over the fire, and eats him.

is_destroyed_by stones [during the escape] The travelers embark in a boat and row away from the shore after blinding the giant. The giant's mates throw stones at it, and one stone eventually knocks it to pieces.

ends_at shore [with the merchant and handicraftsman saved] The shipwreck leaves the merchant and his companions stranded after their ship breaks on the rocks. After the boat is destroyed and his companions drown, the merchant escapes by tying himself to a board and reaching the shore.

A traveller journeys from Redut-Kale toward Anaklia, is overtaken by night and attacked by wolves, and uses sticks on his horse’s tail and a sword to keep them at bay. A light leads him to a lonely house, where a host shelters him and recounts the seven fishermen.
Traveller's horse stands immobile during wolves’ attack, then gallops toward the lonely house when a light appears.
is_a pack [in the forest] The wolves surround the traveller in the forest and try to tear him from his horse. They vanish when a distant light appears.

inhabits lonely house (Mingrelian tale) [near the forest road] The host shelters the traveller in his hut and tells him that his own experiences were worse. He relates how seven fisherman brothers were captured by a one-eyed giant.

is_a seven brothers [all fishermen] The seven brothers are fishermen who are captured by a one-eyed giant after being drawn to a honey stream. The giant eats five of them, while two survive by blinding him and escaping in sheep skins.

Mingrelian fishermen spend months at sea, send catches home weekly, and carry honey and wax after leaving fish. Towed to a rocky shore, they are captured by a one-eyed giant; surviving brothers blind him after he devours most.

is_towed_by giant fish (Mingrelian tale) [after the fishermen’s hooks catch in its gills] The ship is mysteriously pulled away from shore by a giant fish caught on the fishermen’s hooks. After the fishermen escape the giant, they return home in the ship with selected animals from the giant’s flock.

swallows honey stream (Mingrelian tale) [greedily] The giant fish has a mouth a fathom wide and greedily drinks the honey flowing into the sea. Its gills hold the fishermen’s hooks, causing it to tow their ship until they cut their lines.
flows_into Black Sea The honey stream flows from a rocky shore into the sea. The giant fish drinks from it, and the fishermen load their ship with honey and wax.

A one-eyed giant shepherd tends sheep and goats, captures fishermen, confines them in a huge stone building, and roasts and eats them; surviving brothers blind him with a red-hot spit and escape beneath sheep skins.
The giant’s flock, divided into sheep and goats, enables surviving fishermen disguised in sheep skins to select animals and take them aboard their ship.
A huge unhewn stone building has separate rooms for goats, sheep, lambs, and kids; the giant shuts fishermen inside it.

is_used_to_kill Mingrelian fishermen's youngest surviving brother [by the one-eyed giant] The giant uses the spit to roast animals and captured fishermen. Two surviving brothers pull it from the ground, heat it red-hot, and thrust it into the giant’s eye.

l: Mingrelian fishermen's youngest surviving brother, The Library
s: escapes_from one-eyed giant (Mingrelian tale) [with his brother, disguised in sheep skins] He is one of the last two surviving fishermen. He helps blind the giant, disguises himself in a sheep skin, escapes from the building, and reaches the ship.
are_a people [who speak an Iranian tongue] The Ossetes are described as a Caucasian people who speak an Iranian tongue. Their version features Urysmag and a one-eyed giant.

Urysmag, a figure in Ossete and Mingrelian tales, is captured by a one-eyed giant after trying to seize a ram and placed on a roasting spit. He frees himself, blinds the giant, kills the giant’s son, and escapes wearing a ram’s skin.
Two shipwrecked mariners meet a one-eyed giant tending sheep; after one is devoured, the survivor blinds him, escapes in a ram’s skin, and reaches shore on wreckage.

is_a branch of the great Turkish family [widely spread] The Oghuz are presented as a widely spread branch of the Turkish family, including the Turcomans and the Uzbegs of Bokhara. In the Oghuz narrative, the monster Depé Ghoz preys upon them until Bissat undertakes to kill him.

Depé Ghoz is a semi-divine, human-formed one-eyed monster, protected from arrows and swords by his fairy mother’s ring. He devours Oghuz and exacts two men and five hundred sheep daily, captures Bissat, then is blinded, escaped, and beheaded by Bissat.

Bissat, a hero and son of Bissat's mother, sets out to save the Oghuz and avenge his brother, killed by Depé Ghoz. He escapes Depé Ghoz's ox-hide boot, destroys his eye, escapes the cave disguised in a ram's skin, and kills Depé Ghoz.

l: ox-hide boot (Depé Ghoz's boot), The Library
s: is_made_of ox hide [Depé Ghoz’s own boot] Depé Ghoz places Bissat inside his ox-hide boot so that he can roast him later. Bissat cuts the hide with a knife and steps out while the giant sleeps.

protects_against arrows and swords [according to Depé Ghoz’s claim] The ring is said to make its wearer immune to arrows and swords. Depé Ghoz’s fairy mother gives it to him, and later Depé Ghoz offers it to Bissat, but it falls beneath the giant’s feet when Bissat is attacked.

is_interpreted_as sun [by Wilhelm Grimm] Wilhelm Grimm interpreted the eye of Polyphemus as the sun. The text dismisses this interpretation as erroneous and treats the eye instead as part of the imaginative construction of a fairyland giant.
is_sought_by Jason The Golden Fleece is demanded by Jason from Aeetes. Jason wins it with Medea’s aid, flees with her, and later surrenders it to Pelias on returning to Iolcus.
Danae, daughter of Acrisius, is confined in a brazen chamber, conceives Perseus by Zeus, is cast into the sea and reaches Seriphus, is loved by Polydectes, and returns with Perseus to Argos.

Danaus, son of Belus, settles in Libya, where he has fifty daughters and is said to be first to build a ship. He flees with them to Argos, gains its kingdom, permits marriages to sons of Egyptus; his daughters kill their husbands. He gives daughters to athletic-contest victors.
Son of Oedipus and brother of Polynices, Eteocles rules Thebes, breaks their alternating-rule compact, prepares for battle, and is slain by Polynices in single combat.

Europa, daughter of Agenor or Phoenix, is loved by Zeus, who carries her as a bull through the sea to Crete. She bears Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys, is sought by relatives, marries Asterius, gives Harmonia a necklace, and has recorded descendants.

Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus, is born a seven-month child and reigns over Mycenae and Tiryns. After an oracle orders Hercules’ labours, he is served by Hercules, orders the labours, receives several prizes, and refuses some. He hides in a bronze jar, demands Hercules’ sons, wages war with Athenians, and is killed; his sons are slain.

Son of Oeagrus or Apollo and Calliope, Orpheus, an Argonaut famed for music, restrained companions from Sirens, sought Eurydice from Hades, invented Dionysus mysteries, was torn apart by Maenads, buried at Pieria.

The Heraclids, sons of Hercules and members of the family of Inachus, attack and conquer Peloponnese, then leave for Marathon after defeat. Hyllus seeks their return; guided by Oxylus and allied with Pamphylus, they return and finally conquer Peloponnese.

Meleager, son of Oeneus or Ares and Althaea, has a life bound to a burning brand. He hunts the Calydonian boar, gives its skin to Atalanta, kills the sons of Thestius, is in the Argo, dies, and is seen by Hercules in Hades.

The Oracle at Delphi, located at Delphi, gives commands and predictions to many figures and communities. It begins by directing Athamas, warning Pelias, sending Jason concerning the Argo, and ordering Alcmaeon to Achelous, then extends its declarations to kingship, Ilium, Athena, and others.
The Thebans monthly expose sons to the Teumessian vixen, pay Erginus tribute, seek Tiresias’s counsel, resist the Argives, then abandon Thebes after defeat and found Hestiaea.
Description of Greece has title Description of Greece
Description of Greece has author Pausanias
Description of Greece has date 0155~/0175~
Description of Greece has source class canonical
Pericles son of Xanthippus has statue at the Acropolis at Athens (son of Xanthippus)
q: There are also in the Acropolis at Athens statues of Pericles the son of Xanthippus and Xanthippus himself

s: Attalus depicts Amazons (in combat with the Athenians)
q: and the contest between the Amazons and the Athenians

s: Attalus depicts battle of Marathon (against the Persians)
q: and the action at Marathon against the Persians

s: Attalus depicts Galati (in their slaughter in Mysia)
q: and the slaughter of the Galati in Mysia

s: Olympiodorus is illustrious for the greatness of his exploits
q: There too is Olympiodorus, illustrious for the greatness of his exploits

s: battle of Chaeronea is a beginning of sorrows for the Greeks
q: For the disaster at Chæronea was a beginning of sorrows for all the Greeks

s: Philip captured Greek cities (most of them)
q: Most of the Greek cities Philip captured

s: Philip weakened Athens (by taking its islands and ending its naval supremacy)
q: he really hurt them most, robbing them of their islands, and putting down their naval supremacy.

s: Alexander reigns after Philip
q: for some time they were quiet, during the reign of Philip and afterwards of Alexander

s: Aridaeus is successor of Alexander (chosen by the Macedonians after Alexander's death)
q: when Alexander was dead and the Macedonians chose Aridæus as his successor

s: Pericles son of Xanthippus is son of Xanthippus
q: There are also in the Acropolis at Athens statues of Pericles the son of Xanthippus and Xanthippus himself

s: Athenians initiated Lamian War (against Macedonian rule)
q: then the Athenians thought it no longer endurable that Greece should be for all time under Macedonia, but themselves took up arms and urged others to do the same.

s: Leosthenes caused Lamian War (by his death)
q: he infused dejection in all men by his death, and that was the chief reason of their failure.

s: Macedonians occupied Piraeus (after Munychia)
q: For a Macedonian garrison occupied first Munychia, and afterwards the Piræus and the long walls.

s: Demetrius son of Phanostratus was appointed ruler of Athens (by Cassander)
q: and got Demetrius the son of Phanostratus, (who had his father’s repute for wisdom), appointed king over the Athenians.

s: Demetrius deposed Demetrius son of Phanostratus (as ruler of the Athenians)
q: He was however, deposed by Demetrius the son of Antigonus

s: Lachares stripped Athene (of removable ornaments from her statue)
q: he had taken the golden shields from the Acropolis, and had stripped the statue of Athene of all the ornaments that were removable

s: Museum is located in Athens (within the old town walls, on a hill opposite the Acropolis)
q: Now the Museum is within the old town walls, on a hill opposite the Acropolis

s: Museum is associated with Musaeus (Musaeus was said to have sung and died there)
q: where they say that Musæus sang, and died of old age, and was buried.

s: Athenians elected Olympiodorus (as their general)
q: they elected Olympiodorus as their general.

s: Olympiodorus defeated Macedonians (and captured the Museum)
q: And when the Macedonians came out against him he conquered them in battle, and when they fled to the Museum he took it.

s: Olympiodorus recovered the Piræus (and Munychia)
q: though he also recovered the Piræus and Munychia

s: Olympiodorus helped Phocians (when they revolted from Cassander)
q: the Phocians who dwell at Elatea have erected a brazen statue to him at Delphi, because he also helped them when they revolted from Cassander.

s: Eretheum contains Poseidon (an altar also used for sacrifices to Erechtheus)
q: And as you enter there are three altars, one to Poseidon, (on which they also sacrifice to Erechtheus according to the oracle,)

s: Eretheum contains sea water (in a well that roars when the South wind blows)
q: The building is a double one, and inside there is sea water in a well.

s: Poseidon left trident mark in the rock (as proof in his contest with Athene over the territory)
q: And in the rock is the figure of a trident. And this is said to have been Poseidon’s proof in regard to the territory Athene disputed with him.

s: Athene is patron deity of Athens (and of all Attica generally)
q: Sacred to Athene is all the rest of Athens, and similarly all Attica

s: Athene possesses golden lamp of Athene (made by Callimachus; it burns continually for a year when filled with oil)
q: And Callimachus made a golden lamp for the goddess. And when they fill this lamp with oil it lasts for a whole year, although it burns continually night and day.

s: Theseus is son of Ægeus (identified through Aegeus's boots and sword)
q: Ægeus put his boots and sword under a stone as means of identifying his son

s: Theseus's retrieval of Aegeus's tokens is performed by Theseus (at eighteen years of age)
q: Theseus when he was eighteen lifted the stone and removed what Ægeus had left there.

s: Theseus's capture of the Marathonian bull is performed by Theseus (the bull was driven into the Acropolis and sacrificed to Athene)
q: As to the bull that had got to Marathon, it is said to have been driven by Theseus into the Acropolis, and sacrificed to Athene.

s: Attalus depicts giants (in a portrayal of their legendary battle)
q: on the southern wall Attalus has pourtrayed the legendary battle of the giants

s: brazen statue of Athene has visible parts The spearpoint of this Athene, and the plume of her helmet (from Sunium as you sail in)
q: The spearpoint of this Athene, and the plume of her helmet, are visible from Sunium as you sail in.

s: Acropolis has walls built by Pelasgians (except the part built by Cimon)
q: The walls of the Acropolis, (except what Cimon the son of Miltiades built,) are said to have been drawn out by Pelasgians who formerly lived under the Acropolis.

s: Apollo has amour with Creusa daughter of Erechtheus (in a cave below the Propylæa)
q: Here they think Apollo had an amour with Creusa the daughter of Erechtheus.

s: Cylon wins victory at Olympia (in the double course)
q: as he had won the victory at Olympia in the double course

s: Pan is honoured for this message
q: Pan has been honoured therefore for this message.

s: Pan promises aid to Athene (at Marathon)
q: he had said that he was friendly to the Athenians, and would come and help them at Marathon.

s: Philippides meets Pan (near the Parthenian forest)
q: he had met with Pan near the Parthenian forest

s: the Areopagus is named for Ares (because Ares was first tried there)
q: Here is also the Areopagus, so called because Ares was first tried here.

s: Ares is tried at the Areopagus (first trial there)
q: Here is also the Areopagus, so called because Ares was first tried here.

s: Orestes is tried at the Areopagus (for murdering his mother)
q: And they say that subsequently Orestes was tried here for the murder of his mother.

s: Orestes erects altar of Athene (after escaping punishment)
q: And there is an altar of Athene Area, which Orestes erected when he escaped punishment.

s: Æschylus represents Erinnyes (with snakes twined in their hair)
q: Æschylus first represented them with snakes twined in their hair

s: Œdipus has tomb at the Areopagus (his bones were brought from Thebes)
q: Within the precincts is also the tomb of Œdipus. After many enquiries I found that his bones had been brought there from Thebes

s: Cylon marries into Theagenes (as Theagenes' son-in-law)
q: it was his good fortune to wed the daughter of Theagenes the king of Megara.

s: Homer records Mecisteus (as visiting Thebes after Œdipus' death)
q: since Homer records that Mecisteus went to Thebes after the death of Œdipus and was a competitor in the funeral games held in his honour there.

s: Theseus is acquitted for killing Pallas and his sons
q: which was the plea of Theseus when he was acquitted for killing Pallas and his sons who rose up against him.

s: Delos has ship ship (with nine banks of rowers from the decks)
q: But the ship at Delos is the finest I have ever heard of, having nine banks of rowers from the decks.

s: Academy is a gymnasium (formerly belonging to a private man)
